meta.title: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper in Milan | Museum of Ages
meta.description: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper: a wall painting of 4.6 by 8.8 metres in a refectory in Milan, about 1494 to 1498. How it decayed, and what is left.
meta.og_title: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper in Milan
meta.og_image_alt: The Last Supper drawn to one scale beside a person 1.7 metres tall: the wall painting is 4.6 by 8.8 metres. In it the table and, under it, the door's arch where Christ's feet were. A drawing made for this page, the table and the arch after a photograph.

top.answer: The Last Supper is a wall painting. Leonardo da Vinci painted it in Milan, in the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie, the dining hall of a Dominican convent. He painted it for Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, in about 1494 to 1498, and it is still on the wall he painted it on: 4.6 by 8.8 metres, height by width. Look under the table: Christ has no feet. In the seventeenth century the friars wanted a bigger doorway into their kitchens. The one they widened sits in the middle of that wall, right where his feet had been.

blocks.h: How he painted it, and why it began to fail
paras: A wall painting of his time was usually a fresco. The painter works fast on wet plaster, and as the plaster dries it takes the colour in. Leonardo did not want to work fast. The museum explains that he wanted to go slowly and change things as he went. So he let the plaster dry, laid a white ground on it and painted with tempera, much as he would on a wooden panel. A lab study of 2023 found oil in the mix too.

That is why it began to fail. Nothing bound the colour to the wall. It lay on top like a skin, and the room was damp. Within about twenty years it was coming off: in 1517 a visitor already saw the decay. In 1568 Vasari wrote that little could be made out beyond “a glowing stain”, as the museum's site quotes him.

The damage came in waves. In the seventeenth century the friars enlarged the door under the table (a catalogue dates it to 1652), and Christ's feet were lost. In the 1720s a restorer took the picture for an oil painting, a national catalogue says. He washed the wall down with caustic soda, gave it a coat of oil varnish and painted large parts of it anew. In the 1770s it was painted over once more. In 1821 another restorer tried to peel sections off the wall, and failed. Under Napoleon the room was used by troops, as a stable by one account.

Then the war. In August 1943 a bomb exploded in the cloister next door. The refectory lost its roof vault and the wall at its east end. The painted wall held. Since 1940 it had stood behind a steel frame and a thick wall of sandbags, and that shield is what saved it. The room was rebuilt from 1945.

Restorers have been at the wall since the early 1700s, about nine times by the museum's count. For most of that time restoring meant repainting what was missing. In the early 1900s Luigi Cavenaghi restored it, and in the 1950s Mauro Pellicioli secured the flaking surface without taking the old overpaint off.

The last restoration was different. Pinin Brambilla Barcilon began in the late 1970s and finished in 1999, more than twenty years later, and she worked her way across the whole wall. Behind her stood the Milan Soprintendenza and the central restoration institute in Rome, as the press reported. Her team took off the overpaint of the earlier centuries. Under magnification they cleaned what was left of Leonardo's paint, flake by flake, and toned the gaps in watercolour that can be washed off again. Earlier restorers, she reported, had moved eyes, closed mouths and added beards he never painted.
What came back is thin. How much of the paint is still Leonardo's own? The experts' estimates lie between a fifth and a half. No single figure is agreed, and every one of them is an estimate.

The painting is still in its room, which has been a World Heritage Site with the church and the convent since 1980. The air in the refectory is filtered and its climate is controlled. So you enter through a chain of small rooms whose doors open one after the other, and the visits are short, timed and in small groups. Booking is required.

On the wall opposite is a Crucifixion by Giovanni Donato Montorfano. He signed it, dated it 1495 and painted it in fresco. It has kept its colour far better than Leonardo's wall. Kneeling figures of the duke's family were painted onto it later, probably by Leonardo, the museum says, and of them almost nothing is left. For a visit, the museum's own site:

blocks.h: What our copy shows, and what it cannot
paras: The museum's Leonardo wing has a copy of the Last Supper on a wall of its court. It is a reproduction, and it has the original's height and width, 4.6 by 8.8 metres. It shows you two things a book cannot: the size, with you standing in front of it, and the whole composition at once, Christ in the middle and the apostles in four groups of three.

What a flat copy cannot show is the wall itself: the relief of the flakes and the plaster, the state the painting is really in. And it cannot show the room's light. In Milan the painted light comes in from the left, the same side as the real windows of the hall. Take the painting off that wall and the pairing is gone.
